content: World Tuberculosis Day is observed annually on March 24 to raise public awareness about the ongoing global epidemic of tuberculosis (TB), which continues to claim the lives of approximately 1.6 million people each year, predominantly in developing countries. This date marks the anniversary of Dr. Robert Koch's groundbreaking announcement in 1882, when he revealed the discovery of the TB bacillus, the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis. At the time of his announcement in Berlin, TB was a devastating disease, rampant across Europe and the Americas, and was responsible for the death of one in every seven individuals. Dr. Koch's discovery was a pivotal moment in medical history, as it laid the foundation for the diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis. In 1982, to commemorate the centennial of Dr. Koch's discovery, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD) proposed that March 24 be officially recognized as World TB Day. Later, in 1996, the World Health Organization (WHO) partnered with the IUATLD and numerous other organizations to amplify the global impact of World TB Day. In South Africa, the incidence of tuberculosis has tripled in recent years, largely due to the high prevalence of HIV infections in the country. The co-occurrence of HIV and TB has significantly complicated the treatment of tuberculosis. South African patients undergoing the six-month TB treatment regimen are eligible to receive a financial grant during this period. However, there have been instances where treatment is deliberately interrupted in order to extend the duration of grant eligibility.
